corrections.claimed_speedup: Loop-invariant divisor (reciprocal hoisted, 5,000 divrems per call): V8 d8 29.67 us -> 18.24 us (-38.5%), wasmtime 52.51 us -> 13.97 us (-73.4%), native 134.44 us -> 9.73 us (-92.8%). Single divisions: native reciprocal is faster (udivrem128 27.86 ns -> 17.18 ns, -38.3%; -28.5% to -38.3% across the six ops), but on Wasm it is not: V8 +19.6% to +33.4% slower (udivrem128 18.27 ns builtin vs 24.38 ns reciprocal), wasmtime -0.7% to +10.3% (udivrem128 +0.2%).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.0-nightly (61d7280f3 2026-06-06), release profile opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, profile rustflags -Z mir-opt-level=5 -Z inline-mir=yes -Z cross-crate-inline-threshold=always; native x86_64 built with -C target-cpu=native; wasm32 target features +bulk-memory,+multivalue,+reference-types,+wide-arithmetic with build-std (compiler-builtins rebuilt with the same features); criterion 0.8.2 (300 samples, 3 s measurement); d8 15.1.52; wasmtime 45.0.1
corrections.caveats: Mixed result by design: the reciprocal path wins on Wasm only when the divisor is loop-invariant and the reciprocal is hoisted by hand (the bench calls recip128 once before the loop; the builtin libcall cannot be hoisted); for one-off divisions the builtin is faster on V8 and about equal on wasmtime. Each single-op bench times one fixed seeded operand pair, so it measures one kernel path with warm branch predictors. The loop-invariant workload is narrow: one seeded divisor in (0, 2^127) whose high word equals the dividend's high word up to the low 13 bits and the top bit, so quotients are 0 or small and the reciprocal path's Y > X shortcut can fire. The native -92.8% probably reflects a slow native __udivti3 (likely the hardware 128/64 DIV path on this Coffee Lake laptop CPU; verifier inference): the same builtin compiled to Wasm takes 77.9% less time on the loop under d8 than natively (134.44 us native vs 29.67 us d8). Baseline is Rust's compiler-builtins (__udivti3/__umodti3), not TypeScript/JS or Emscripten C++. Single macOS laptop; research micro-benchmark and proposal sketch (extended wide-arithmetic i64.recip128/i64.divrem_recip128), not a library; no license file, 0 stars. Correctness of the reciprocal loop is checked against native division by a unit test (divrem_with_loop_invariant_divisor_matches_native).

tier_reason: Code (mul_mats.js, mul_mats.c, mul_mats_intrin.c, Dockerfile), compilers, flags and CPU (i5-1135G7) are all public, but the JavaScript baseline is broken: mul_mats.js never initialises its input arrays, so every product is undefined*undefined = NaN on holey generic arrays with no result check, and it does double arithmetic while the C/Wasm side does int32. A baseline with an unfixed correctness bug that also understates idiomatic JS caps the claim at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (first-party, Node.js v16.16.0): mul_mats_intrin-wasm-simd-O3 0.245s vs mul_mats.js 5.768s (-95.8%, about 23.5x, derived from page data); -O3 -msimd128 auto-vectorised 0.278s (-95.2%); -O3 without SIMD 2.012s (-65%); Wasm built without -O3 (emcc default -O0) is slower than JS (6.865s, +19%). The JS baseline computes NaN on uninitialised arrays; in a verifier rerun on Node 22.22.0 (different machine, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz) the repo's JS took 10.342s while an Int32Array version with a local accumulator and Math.imul took 4.583s (2.26x faster), so against idiomatic JS the headline would be roughly 10x, not 23.5x (estimate, cross-machine).
corrections.caveats: Baseline defect: mul_mats.js allocates in_a.arr and in_b.arr with new Array(size) and never fills them (its transpose loop writes to the wrapper objects, not .arr), so the timed loop multiplies undefined*undefined = NaN in holey arrays and the output is never checked; the C/Wasm versions fill inputs with 1 and verify the sum. JS uses doubles while C/Wasm use int32 (wasm_i32x4_mul). Verifier rerun on Node 22.22.0: original 10.342s (sum NaN), filled plain arrays 9.876s, Int32Array 6.660s, Int32Array with local accumulator 4.583s; the uninitialised arrays cost little, but the untyped, store-every-iteration JS understates JS by about 2.3x. The intrinsics kernel had an indexing bug fixed on 2022-09-01 (fa08bf6, loads from &in_a[i] instead of &in_a[i*n+k]); that commit re-measured the two -O3 SIMD rows (0.062s became 0.245s) but not the non-O3 intrinsics row (4.718s), which predates the fix. Non-O3 Wasm rows are emcc -O0 debug builds. Native GCC -O3 is baseline x86-64 (SSE2, no pmulld), so Wasm SIMD beating it is a flags artifact; native -O3 -mavx2 (0.119s) is about 2x faster than the best Wasm row. Single 64x64 int32 matrix-multiply microbenchmark from a 2022 Node 16 / Emscripten 3.1.18 setup; demo repo for a blog post, not a library.

notes: Numbers match the README, but the JS baseline never initialises its inputs (computes NaN, unchecked) and is untyped double code vs int32 Wasm; verifier rerun shows idiomatic typed JS 2.26x faster than the repo's JS, so the 23.5x headline is overstated (roughly 10x). Not invalid enough to reject (the Wasm side does the real work and is verified by its sum check). Metadata: MIT, 13 stars, 0 forks, last commit 2022-09-01 (abandoned), not a fork.
